subsection: 2. The second Sinn Féin, the 1918 election and the War of Independence, 1917–1921

notes.h: The rise of the second Sinn Féin, 1917
notes.b: Sinn Féin was founded by Arthur Griffith in 1905 on a policy of abstention from Westminster and a dual-monarchy model. After 1916 it was reorganised under new leadership and a republican programme.
points: Arthur Griffith founded Sinn Féin in 1905, promoting abstention from Westminster and a self-governing Ireland under the Crown, on the model of Hungary's relationship with Austria.
Count Plunkett won the North Roscommon by-election in February 1917 as a Sinn Féin candidate, the first by-election win of the rising movement.
Éamon de Valera won East Clare in July 1917, and Joseph McGuinness won South Longford in August 1917.
At the Sinn Féin Ard Fheis in October 1917 the party adopted a republican constitution and elected de Valera as its president.
The new Sinn Féin absorbed many former Volunteers and the IRB; Griffith remained the party's leading thinker but was overshadowed by de Valera's leadership.
The party's aims were an Irish republic and the recognition of Irish sovereignty by the peace conference, with abstention from Westminster as its method.

notes.h: The conscription crisis and the German Plot, 1918
notes.b: In spring 1918 the British government's plan to extend conscription to Ireland, after the German offensive in France, gave Sinn Féin mass support and led to repression of the party.
points: The Military Service Act of April 1918 extended conscription to Ireland, though it was never enforced in the country.
Nationalist parties, the Catholic hierarchy and Sinn Féin united in opposing conscription, and an anti-conscription pledge was widely signed in April 1918.
A one-day general strike and a mass protest took place on 23 April 1918 in response to conscription.
The British government claimed in May 1918 that Sinn Féin had conspired with Germany in what was called the German Plot.
De Valera, Arthur Griffith and other Sinn Féin leaders were arrested in May 1918 and held in prisons in England and Ireland.
John Redmond, leader of the Irish Parliamentary Party, died in March 1918, a month before the conscription bill, and the Parliamentary Party's influence collapsed after the crisis.

notes.b: The December 1918 election was the first held on the new franchise and gave Sinn Féin a commanding position in Irish seats, while its MPs refused to sit at Westminster.
points: Sinn Féin won 73 of Ireland's 105 Westminster seats in the December 1918 general election.
The Irish Parliamentary Party won six seats, a collapse from its position before 1914.
Unionists held most of the seats in the north-east, reflecting the territorial division that partition would later formalise.
Many Sinn Féin candidates were in prison during the campaign, and de Valera won East Clare from Lincoln Gaol before escaping in February 1919.
Constance Markievicz won St Patrick's, Dublin, becoming the first woman elected to the House of Commons, but she did not take her seat.
The Sinn Féin MPs refused to attend Westminster and instead met in Dublin as the First Dáil.

notes.h: The First Dáil and the Declaration of Independence, 1919
notes.b: The First Dáil met at the Mansion House, Dublin, on 21 January 1919, and asserted an Irish republic and a government outside British control.
points: The First Dáil met on 21 January 1919 at the Mansion House in Dublin, and only a minority of the elected members attended.
The assembly adopted a Declaration of Independence, and a Democratic Programme setting out social and economic aims for the new state.
The Dáil elected de Valera as President in April 1919, while he was in prison, and it formed a ministry of its own.
Michael Collins became Minister for Finance, Arthur Griffith became Minister for Home Affairs, and Constance Markievicz became Minister for Labour.
Markievicz was the first woman cabinet minister in Europe, a distinction often claimed for her in 1919.
The Dáil raised money through the Dáil Loan in 1919, and the British government proclaimed the Dáil illegal on 12 September 1919.
Irish Volunteers became known as the Irish Republican Army (IRA) in 1919, and the IRA became the military arm of the Dáil's government.

notes.b: The War of Independence was a guerrilla campaign by the IRA against the police and British forces, combined with a political campaign for recognition of the Dáil.
points: The first shots were fired at Soloheadbeg, Co. Tipperary, on 21 January 1919, when IRA men led by Seán Treacy and Dan Breen killed two RIC constables guarding a gelignite delivery.
The IRA worked in flying columns, small mobile units which attacked police barracks, ambushed patrols and sought to make Irish counties ungovernable for the British.
Michael Collins ran an intelligence network in Dublin and organised a group of assassins known as the Squad, which targeted detectives and agents.
The Dáil set up its own courts, the Dáil Courts, from 1920, which settled disputes and competed with British courts for authority.

On Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920, the Squad killed about fourteen British intelligence officers in Dublin; later that afternoon British forces fired on the crowd at Croke Park, killing about fourteen people.
Kevin Barry, an IRA volunteer, was hanged in Mountjoy Prison on 1 November 1920, becoming a republican martyr.
At Kilmichael, Co. Cork, on 28 November 1920, a flying column under Tom Barry ambushed a patrol of Auxiliaries and killed seventeen of them.
British forces burned much of Cork city centre on 11–12 December 1920 in reprisal for IRA attacks.

notes.h: British counter-measures: Black and Tans and Auxiliaries, 1920–1921
notes.b: The British response relied on reinforcing the Royal Irish Constabulary with ex-soldiers, which increased violence and reprisals.
points: The Royal Irish Constabulary was reinforced from early 1920 by ex-soldiers recruited as temporary constables, known as the Black and Tans from their mixed uniforms.
The Auxiliary Division of the RIC, a force of ex-officers, was recruited from mid-1920 and became notorious for reprisals.
The Restoration of Order in Ireland Act (August 1920) gave the authorities power to impose martial law and to try people by military courts.
Reprisals included the burning of creameries, the sacking of towns and the shooting of civilians, and British reprisals drew criticism in Britain and abroad.
Martial law covered much of the south and west, and many IRA prisoners were held in British camps and prisons.

notes.b: Collins was the Dáil's most effective organiser and the IRA's intelligence chief. He was a participant in the Rising, a leader of the War of Independence and a negotiator of the Treaty.
points: Collins (1890–1922) was born at Sam's Cross, Co. Cork, worked in London in the post office and the civil service, and joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood.
He fought in the GPO during the Rising in 1916 and was interned at Frongoch in Wales afterwards.
He organised the Dáil Loan in 1919, served as Minister for Finance, and became Director of Intelligence for the IRA.
His Squad and intelligence network helped to kill British agents in Dublin, and he was a key architect of the IRA's guerrilla strategy in 1919–21.
He was one of the Irish plenipotentiaries who negotiated the Treaty in London in late 1921, a role considered in the notes on the Treaty negotiations.
Contemporaries split: supporters saw him as the leader who won independence, while British officials and anti-Treaty republicans regarded him as a ruthless organiser.

Historians such as Tim Pat Coogan, in his 1990 biography, portray him as a pragmatic leader who accepted the Treaty as a means to further freedom, while others see him as the architect of the Free State.

notes.b: This part of de Valera's career covers his leadership of Sinn Féin and the Dáil before the Treaty. His later career is covered in the notes on the Free State and the Republic.
points: De Valera (1882–1975) was born in New York, raised in Bruree, Co. Limerick, and worked as a mathematics teacher before joining the Irish Volunteers.
He commanded the Volunteers at Boland's Mill during the Rising; his death sentence was commuted because he had been born in the United States.
He was released in June 1917 and became president of Sinn Féin in October 1917, and he was elected President of the Dáil in April 1919.
He escaped from Lincoln Gaol in February 1919, and he travelled to the United States from June 1919 to December 1920 to raise funds and to seek American recognition for the Irish republic.
Contemporaries admired his stature and his ability to hold Sinn Féin together, but British officials and some Irish nationalists were wary of his uncompromising republicanism.
Historians such as Diarmaid Ferriter, in his 2007 biography Judging Dev, judge him as a skilled politician whose republican stance could be both inflexible and pragmatic.

notes.b: This part covers Markievicz's role in the Dáil and the War of Independence after her release in 1917.
points: After her release in June 1917 she toured Ireland for Sinn Féin, speaking in favour of an Irish republic and the Dáil.
She was elected for St Patrick's, Dublin, in 1918 but did not take her seat at Westminster, and she sat as a member of the First Dáil.
As Minister for Labour in 1919 she supported workers' rights and the Democratic Programme's social aims.
She was arrested in the German Plot round-up of 1918 and held in prison in England before being released in 1919.
She took the anti-Treaty side in the Civil War and was imprisoned by the Free State in 1923, a stage in her career discussed in the notes on the Civil War.
Contemporaries saw her as a figure of theatrical nationalism; historians often treat her as a pioneer of women's political participation in Ireland.

notes.h: Assessment: the Sinn Féin mandate and the War of Independence
notes.b: Judgements on the period depend on whether the 1918 result, the Dáil and the IRA campaign are seen as a mandate, as a military success, or as a set of costs that brought a compromise.
points: Sinn Féin's 1918 victory gave the Dáil a democratic mandate that the British could not easily ignore, and it changed the terms of the Irish question.
The IRA's guerrilla campaign inflicted heavy losses on the RIC and made Irish counties costly to govern, which helped bring Britain to the negotiating table.
Critics argue that the IRA's targeting of civilians and informers, and the British reprisals, caused grave suffering that the settlement of 1921 did not justify.
Historians differ over whether the War of Independence was a people's war with broad support or a campaign carried on by a minority of activists.
The Truce of 11 July 1921 followed a British decision, prompted by Lloyd George's letter to de Valera of 24 June 1921, to hold talks rather than continue the campaign.
The Dáil's dual approach, with its political institutions and its armed wing, shaped the Free State's divisions over the Treaty in the months that followed.

keyTerms.definition: A state with no monarch at its head, which Sinn Féin, the Dáil and the anti-Treaty IRA all demanded for Ireland.
Supreme authority over a state's own affairs, which the Dáil claimed for Ireland in 1919 and the Treaty later qualified.
The Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret republican society, and the Irish Republican Army, the armed force of the Dáil from 1919.
The Irish parliament that the Sinn Féin MPs set up in January 1919, claiming to be the legitimate government of Ireland.
The social and economic programme adopted by the First Dáil in January 1919, promising reforms for workers, farmers and the poor.
The courts set up by the Dáil from 1920 to settle disputes, which competed with the British legal system.
Small, mobile IRA units that carried out ambushes and attacks on police and military targets in the War of Independence.
Temporary constables recruited from ex-soldiers in 1920 to reinforce the Royal Irish Constabulary, known for reprisals against civilians.
The Auxiliary Division of the RIC, a force of ex-officers recruited in 1920 whose ambush at Kilmichael became notorious.
The ceasefire agreed on 11 July 1921 between the British government and the IRA, which led to the Treaty negotiations.
